Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: This item appears misclassified within the Threat node because it describes an avoidance behaviour rather than a threat appraisal or sense of current danger. Given the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Maladaptive Strategies, so threat items should plausibly drive coping responses; this item itself is already a maladaptive strategy and duplicates the behavioural content of the Maladaptive Strategies node. The other Threat items (flashbacks, scanning exits) reflect re-experiencing/current danger more coherently for torture trauma.

vignette:
Priya was twenty-two when she was detained - a young tailor's apprentice in a city that had become suddenly unrecognizable. For three weeks, she was held in a basement room where guards took turns humiliating and hurting her. They told her that showing any emotion would earn her an extra session, so she learned to keep her face blank even when the pain made her want to scream. She learned not to relax, because the moment she slumped against the wall they would kick her awake and say she was too comfortable. Even medical care was weaponised: when she developed an infection from a wound, a guard forced a needle into her arm without cleaning the skin, laughing as she flinched. She survived, was released, and fled to the United States with her husband.

Six years later, Priya works as a tailor in a small shop, but the basement has never really left her. A sudden noise - the clatter of a metal rack - brings the smell of damp concrete back so vividly that for a second she is there again, heart pounding, scanning the walls for a way out. She scans for exits constantly: every room she enters, every shop, every bus. She is superalert to the people around her, reading their hands and their tone of voice for the first sign of cruelty. These moments of hypervigilance and flashbacks come without warning, and they have reshaped how she lives. Because the threat feels so immediate, she has built her days around avoiding anything that might leave her vulnerable. She refuses to see a doctor even for routine checkups - the thought of a waiting room, of a stranger in a white coat, makes her chest tighten until she cannot breathe. She has not had a pap smear or a blood test since arriving in the US, and last year when she pricked her finger badly on a sewing needle, she wrapped it in a strip of cloth and did not go to the clinic. Strong emotions, too, feel dangerous: when a customer complained angrily about a hem, Priya felt the old freeze response take over and later cancelled all the woman's future appointments rather than risk another interaction. Even pleasant feelings set her on edge - she ends phone calls with her mother abruptly when she feels herself growing warm with love, because loving someone once made her a target. And relaxation itself has come to feel like a trap. She does not sit down during her lunch break; she stands by the door, watching the street. On weekends she keeps cleaning or sewing until she is exhausted, because the moment she stops, the vigilance creeps in worse. Her husband has tried to persuade her to take a day off, to let him take her to a doctor for a persistent cough, but Priya cannot explain why every offer of help feels like a trick.

What finally brought her to seek help was a flashback that landed her on the floor of her shop, gasping, while a customer called an ambulance. Paramedics found no physical emergency, but the terror in her eyes led them to recommend a therapist. Priya is here now, dreading that if she lets herself feel safe, something terrible will happen again - and equally afraid that she will spend the rest of her life trapped in a basement that no longer exists.
